newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 4.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 4.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. -- BUDGET FAILS TO CHECK STERLING

Despite chancellor Gordon Brown's claims of a tough Budget, sterling continued to soar through its former central rate in the European exchange mechanism on Thursday. Brown believed his Budget provided sufficient incentive for reducing consumer spending and re-balancing the economy, but fears that the Bank of England would once again raise interest rates sharply led sterling to rise to over DM2.96 in trading late on Thursday - over eight pfennigs higher than when Brown began his Wednesday budget speech.
-- UTILITIES PROTEST AT LEVY'S 'EXCESS PROFITS' FORMULA

Though several of the major utilities continue to express discontent over the government's new windfall tax, it now appears there will be no legal battles over the levy. BG, one of the most heavily taxed utilities, revealed it is continuing to study figures, but signalled it was 'not predisposed to challenge a tax for which the government has a popular mandate. American owners of British Utilities have also indicated they will seek no action against the imposition of the windfall tax.
-- HEAVY BURDEN PROMPTS HYDER TO REASSESS FINANCES

Welsh water and electricity group Hyder has reacted to its estimated 282 million sterling windfall tax burden by launching a 'fundamental review' of its finances. Hyder was one of the few utilities to fall on the stock market on Thursday, as investors were worried Hyder would be issuing shares to help pay for its large bill. Water industry regulator Ofwat has emphasised that it will not condone the practice of customers sharing the windfall tax burden.
-- ABOLITION OF FIDS MAY FORCE COMPANIES OFFSHORE

Multinational businesses and London analysts have warned that the government's decision to abolish foreign income dividends beginning in 1999 may lead to some companies choosing to relocate their businesses overseas. The abolition of fids will result in some companies having to pay double taxation on their dividends, a prospect which does not appeal to groups such as Rio Tinto mining, Allied Domecq, B.A.T, Glaxo Wellcome, SmithKline Beecham, Burmah Castrol and Lasmo. The Inland Revenue estimates that the measure will raise about 250 million sterling.
-- UNOFFICIAL STRIKES 'COMMON IN SERVICE SECTOR'

A study by Gregor Gall at Stirling University and Sonia McKay at the independent Labour Research Department has shown that unofficial strikes remain common in Britain and are more likely to occur within the service sector than the manufacturing and energy industries. The latest data from the Confederation of British Industry and the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply has revealed that consumer spending is continuing 'to romp ahead'. Both surveys indicate continued high levels of spending and business activity for June, figures which will now most likely be examined by the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee. The survey carried out by the CBI, which covers 15,000 retailing and wholesaling outlets, shows rises in all retailing sectors except footwear and leather goods, with the best performances coming from the housing market, such as furniture, carpets and household goods.
-- DISPLAY.IT SHARES FALL 20 PER CENT

Shares in UK software venture Display.IT fell by 20 per cent on the Ofex over- the-counter market on Thursday amid concerns about the credibility of the company's sales forecasts. The company had risen spectacularly on the back of enthusiasm for the Internet, increasing its market value 40-fold within its first year. It had been presented by its own PR company as a challenger to financial information groups such as Reuters, but the current difficulties highlight the problems in valuing Internet start-ups.
-- GALEN FLOTATION PRICE TO BE 150P

Northern Ireland pharmaceuticals company Galen will be valued at 181.9 million stg for its flotation next week. The company has announced a placing price of 150p for the issue, which seeks to raise a total of 45.4 million stg. The bulk of the new money will fund expansion of the company's drug services business, investment in facilities in the US and Northern Ireland, and clinical trials of its intra-vaginal ring which administers HRT hormones.
-- BRUSSELS PROBES DEAL TO TRANSFER STAKE IN LONRHO

A European Commission inquiry has begun into the proposed deal by which South African mining combine Anglo American would transfer control of a 26.7 per cent stake in the UK's Lonrho to JCI, South Africa's first black-run mining group. The Commission had originally objected to Anglo's purchase of the stake in Lonrho, arguing that it would give the South African group an excessive influence in the world platinum market. The current investigation follows the news this week that JCI had acquired an option to buy the Lonrho stake from Anglo.
-- UNITED UTILITIES CHANGES PAY PLAN

After conducting 'extensive further consultations' with shareholders, United Utilities has introduced proposals for a modification in its long-term pay scheme for executive directors. The group will now compare its performance with that of other utility groups and the FTSE 100, basing short-term awards on the current year and not a rolling three year average. Shareholders had threatened to reject last year's proposal which was called 'over-generous and over-complex' by the Association of British Insurers, and a voter turnout on the decision of only 37.5 per cent led to United's promise of a review into the issue.
